newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - March 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - March 1.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
Financial Express
INDUSTRY UNANIMOUS IN HAILING BUDGET

Industrial chambers unanimously supported the finance minister's second budget, terming it growth-oriented, investor-friendly, progressive and forward-looking. Abolition of the corporate surcharge, reduction in corporate and personal tax rates, rationalisation of duties, removal of double taxation on dividend and replacement of the foreign exchange regulations were received enthusiastically by the industry. The industry also hailed the announcements of allowing buy-back of shares, amendment in the urban land ceiling regulations and raising the standard deduction limit in personal income tax.
DEFENCE OUTLAY GETS 66 BLN RUPEE JUMP

In an attempt to reduce the deficit in the defence budget, the finance minister raised the outlay for defence. It would now be 356.2 billion rupees, registering an increase of about 66 billion rupees over the 1996/97 (April-March) allocation. The hike was well over 20 percent over the previous year's revised estimates and catered for the 8 percent inflation.
SMALL SCALE SECTOR TAX RATE SIMPLIFIED, 14 ITEMS DERESERVED

The tax structure for the small sector (SSI) was simplified and credit flow eased. Simultaneously, 14 items mainly in the agricultural sector were dereserved to pave way for multinational and corporate investment. Texturised man-made yarn and cotton yarn were also excluded from the purview of the SSI exemption scheme. The duty exemption granted to jams, jellies and sauces were withdrawn and these would now invite eight percent duty. Small scale units were granted full exemption from duty on clearances up to three million rupees in a financial year. Beyond that up to 10 million, SSIs would pay duty on a flat rate.
TAX HOLIDAY EXTENDED TO TELECOM SECTOR

The finance minister extended the tax holiday benefits to the telecom sector as given to the infrastructure sector. Other benefits extended to telecom were amortisation of licence fees, inclusion of investments in debentures and equity shares of a public telecom company for the purposes of tax rebate. Tripartite agreements were proposed among the Department of Telecommunications, the licencees and the lenders on the issue of telecom licensing. Duty on parts of cellular phones and pagers was reduced from 30 to 20 percent and on telecom equipment from 40 to 30 percent and on their parts from 30 to 20 percent.
NOTHING TO BOOST POWER

The finance minister offered little to boost the power sector, though in his budget speech he expressed concern over the sluggish performance of the sector. The only concession for power was in the form of a reduced duty on non-coking coal, from 20 percent to 10 percent. This would help cash starved hydro and thermal power companies in the public sector in particular. Similarly, concessions given to the gas industry would also boost gas based power companies.
HEALTH INSURANCE OPENED TO PRIVATE SECTOR

Health insurance was opened up to the private sector, with foreign firms allowed to hold minority stake. The government insurance monopolies LIC and GIC were allowed to float joint ventures and were given freedom to determine service conditions of their employees and agents. Although nothing was mentioned about allowing foreign insurance companies in this sector, only a few companies, with majority Indian ownership, would be permitted to enter the health insurance sector.
Business Standard
CORPORATE TAX RATE CUT TO 35 PERCENT

The finance minister announced sharp cuts in corporate taxes and restructured the minimum alternate tax (MAT). Basic corporate tax rates for Indian companies were cut from 40 to 35 percent and the 7.5 percent tax surcharge abolished. Tax rate on foreign companies was also brought down from 55 to 48 percent. Certain changes in the 19.5 percent MAT was also proposed. Export profits were exempted from MAT and a system of deferred tax credit introduced. Tax credit earned by a company (while paying MAT) would be allowed to be carried forward for five years. When the company started paying regular tax, it would be allowed to set off the tax credit earned by paying MAT.
STOCKS SURGE ON HECTIC BUYING

Stocks spiralled upwards in two hours of hectic post-budget trading as investors shovelled money into the market to greet the market-friendly measures announced by the finance minister. The Bombay bourse index surged 261 points to 3735, before profit-taking by speculators brought it down to 3652.99 at close. The local broking community and foreign institutional investors were upbeat over the package and prophesied a buoyant phase in the week ahead.
MARKETS CHEER HISTORIC BUDGET

The finance minister unveiled a budget with substantial incentives for the corporate sector that sent stock markets soaring and put industry in an upbeat mood. The budget measures included containment of the fiscal deficit to the target five percent, with expenditure kept within budget limits. The reform process was taken several steps forward, including in the farm sector. Futures trading would be reintroduced in cotton and jute, and restrictive laws on activities like milling would be repealed. Pension funds were opened up, initially to the state-owned Unit Trust of India.
STATES TO GET 29 PCT SHARE OF SINGLE TAX POOL

The finance minister, resolving a long-standing demand of the states, promised a single pool of divisible taxes. Presently, not all taxes are shared. The union government keeps all of customs duties, 52.5 percent of excise duties and 22.5 percent of income taxes. This was a major bone of contention between the states and the union. In November 1994 a finance panel, convened every five years to determine the states' share of taxes, recommended a single pool of divisible taxes. It had also recommended the states should get 29 percent of the single pool.
MANAGEMENTS MADE FREE TO DECIDE SHAREHOLDING

A major policy initiative taken by the finance minister would free corporate managements to review and decide the composition of shareholding in their companies. It would also give them partial freedom to manage their funds, increase accountability through greater disclosures to shareholders and strengthen corporate democracy through greater empowerment of shareholders. Procedures were also being eased for minority shareholders through provisions for nomination facility, while measures were taken for professionalising the broker network.
FOREIGN INVESTORS SEEN EYEING STOCKS AFRESH

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) would be eyeing Indian stocks again, with the aggregate ceiling limit for FIIs being raised to 30 percent against the existing 24 percent. A large section of the FIIs were of the view that the investment decisions would be sector specific in the coming months. The future favourites would be telecom, software, power and bank stocks. The FII community, however, expressed fears over how the figures would be matched and where additional revenue would come from. In this connection, FIIs were of the view that the disinvestment programme of government-firms, scheduled for 1997/98, would need to be more aggressive.
The Observer
NEW EXPLORATION LICENSING POLICY UNVEILED

The finance minister announced a new exploration licensing policy (NELP), in a bid to attract foreign investment in the oil sector. National oil companies would now be paid the international price of oil for new discoveries made under the NELP. Royalty payments would be fixed on an ad valorem basis, with royalty payments for exploration in deep waters to be charged at half the rate for offshore areas in the first seven years of commercial production. The oil companies would be free to market crude oil and natural gas produced by them. AD HOC TREASURY BILLS ABOLISHED

The budget announced the decision to discontinue the ad hoc treasury bills. The central bank (RBI) and the government proposed the system of ad hoc treasury bills to finance budget deficit would be discontinued from April 1, 1997. A scheme of Ways and Means Advances (WMA) by RBI to the government would be introduced to accommodate temporary mismatches in government receipts and payments.
FINANCE MINISTER WIDENS TAX NET IN BUDGET

The finance minister sought to widen the tax net by making it mandatory for those owning cars, telephones and immobile property in metropolitan cities and foreign travellers to file income tax returns. The budget also sought to enlarge the scope of service tax to cover consultant engineers, goods transporters, car rentals, tour operators, outdoor caterers, and recruitment agencies. The minister also announced a voluntary disclosure scheme to tap unaccounted wealth for productive purposes by which any disclosed income would be taxed at the revised highest rate of 30 percent.
Business Line
SIEMENS MAY PROVIDE CONTROL PANELS

Russia planned to rope in German engineering giant Siemens to provide the latest control panels for the $2.6 billion worth two 1,000 megawatt nuclear reactors it has agreed to sell to India. The two pressurised water reactors (PWR) for the proposed Kudankulam Atomic Power Project in Tamil Nadu would be executed on terms similar to the one implemented by Russia in Finland recently. Though the Finnish reactor was smaller, a similar approach of providing Russian reactor and technology along with the Siemens control panel would most likely be worked out with India also.
WHEN PARTS WILL COST MORE THAN THE SUM

The 1997/98 budget proposals brought back the anomaly of the inverted duty structure. This anomaly, which crept in two years back, was rectified to a large extent in the previous two budgets. The 1997/98 budget reduced the import duty for complete machinery from 25 percent to 20 percent. Except for CR coils, no such corresponding reduction was announced for components and raw materials. This would adversely impact operations of the domestic machinery manufacturers as it would now be cheaper to import complete machinery rather than buy it in the domestic market.
